title: Check yourself: the Single Responsibility Principle

questions.stem: A `ParcelDesk` class has `postage(parcel)`, whose rates the carrier-contracts team sets, and `labelText(parcel)`, whose layout the warehouse team sets. Both call a private `weightKg(parcel)` that rounds the weight up to the next 100 g. The warehouse asks for labels to show the weight to the gram, so a developer removes the rounding from `weightKg`; the label's test is updated and passes. What happens to postage?

options.text: It changes for parcels between two 100 g steps, since postage is now computed from the weight without the round-up
options.says: postage reads the weight through the same private helper, so the warehouse's change reaches the contracts team's rates

options.text: It changes for parcels at an exact 100 g step, since those are the weights the round-up used to leave alone
options.says: a weight already on a 100 g step is the same with or without the round-up; the weights in between are the ones that move

options.text: It stays the same, since the request came from the warehouse team and postage answers to the contracts team
options.says: who asked doesn't limit what the change reaches; the two actors meet in the helper they share

options.text: It stays the same, since the edit was made in a private method that only the label's test covers
options.says: a private helper called by both methods is shared code; which test covers it doesn't decide what it changes

origin.section: A Reason to Change Is an Actor Who Asks for It

questions.stem: A hotel booking class was split into `RoomPricing`, which the revenue team owns, and `ConfirmationEmail`, which the marketing team owns. Both get the length of a stay from a static `Dates.nights(checkIn, checkOut)`. Marketing asks for the email to count days instead of nights ("your 4-day stay" for three nights), and the developer adds one to the result of `Dates.nights`, since the email calls it. What happens to room prices?

options.text: They rise by one night, since `RoomPricing` still reads the length of stay through the method that was changed
options.says: the utility answers to both actors, so the marketing change reaches pricing as it would inside one class

options.text: They rise by one night, since `ConfirmationEmail` and `RoomPricing` were split from one class and still change together
options.says: what ties them is the utility both call, not the fact that they were split from one class; classes split by actor stop changing together

options.text: They stay the same, since the split already gave the revenue team and the marketing team a class each
options.says: separate classes help only when no code that one actor's request changes is called by the other

options.text: They stay the same, since a utility class belongs to no team and its methods are neutral between them
options.says: a utility called by two actors answers to both; a change for one reaches the other

origin.section: Moving Methods into Separate Classes Fixes Nothing While the Actors Share a Helper

questions.stem: In a billing codebase, `TaxRules` has 14 public methods, and every change to it in two years was asked for by the tax team. `InvoiceCsv` has 2: `export(invoices)`, whose columns the accounting system's team defines, and `importSupplierPrices(file)`, whose format the purchasing team agrees with suppliers. A reviewer has time to split one of them. Which one, and why?

options.text: `InvoiceCsv`, since requests from two different teams change its two methods
options.says: a reason to change is an actor; InvoiceCsv answers to two, TaxRules to one

options.text: `InvoiceCsv`, since its two methods do two different things, writing a file and reading one
options.says: verbs don't measure a responsibility; the split is justified by the two teams, not by the two operations

options.text: `TaxRules`, since its 14 methods give the tax team 14 reasons to ask for a change
options.says: the number of methods doesn't measure a responsibility; 14 methods changed by one team are one reason

options.text: `TaxRules`, since each of the tax team's rules could then be tested in a class of its own
options.says: splitting one actor's rules into a class per step moves the way they combine into every caller

origin.section: Splitting by Verb Instead of by Actor Moves the Rule into Every Caller

questions.stem: A grocer's pricing is split into one-method classes: `Coupon.apply(amount)` takes 10.00 off, and `Delivery.add(amount)` adds a 4.90 fee below 50.00 and nothing from 50.00. The checkout computes `delivery.add(coupon.apply(basket))`. The mobile app's basket screen, written later, computes `coupon.apply(delivery.add(basket))`. Both classes' tests pass. A customer with a 55.00 basket and a coupon reads the app, then pays. What do they see?

options.text: The app shows 45.00 and the checkout charges 49.90, since each caller decides whether the fee is judged before or after the coupon
options.says: the app judges the fee on 55.00 (none) and then takes 10.00 off; the checkout takes 10.00 off first, so 45.00 is below 50.00 and the fee is added

options.text: The app shows 49.90 and the checkout charges 45.00, since each caller decides whether the fee is judged before or after the coupon
options.says: the amounts are the other way round: the checkout applies the coupon first, so its fee is judged on 45.00

options.text: Both show 49.90, since the two callers are built from the same step classes and those classes' tests pass
options.says: correct steps don't fix the order they run in; each caller wired its own

options.text: Both show 45.00, since the two callers are built from the same step classes and those classes' tests pass
options.says: correct steps don't fix the order they run in; the checkout's order adds the fee

origin.section: Splitting by Verb Instead of by Actor Moves the Rule into Every Caller
